question.prompt: Given the linear fractional transformation \[ f_1(x)=\frac{2x-1}{x+1}, \] define \(f_{n+1}(x)=f_1(f_n(x))\) for \(n=1,\) \(2,\) \(3,\) \(\ldots.\) Assuming \(f_{35}(x)=f_5(x),\) it follows that \(f_{28}(x)\) is equal to:

solutions.explanation:
Because every step applies the same function, a short cycle can replace twenty-eight separate substitutions. We must also retain inputs excluded by intermediate denominators.

Starting with \(x\ne-1\), the second iterate simplifies to
\[
f_2(x)=\frac{2(2x-1)-(x+1)}{(2x-1)+(x+1)}
=\frac{x-1}{x}.
\]
This step additionally excludes \(x=0\). Continuing to substitute each result into \(f_1\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_3(x)&=\frac{x-2}{2x-1},\\
f_4(x)&=\frac{1}{1-x},\\
f_5(x)&=\frac{x+1}{2-x},\\
f_6(x)&=x.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each new step requires the preceding value to be different from \(-1\). The third, fourth, and fifth steps additionally exclude \(x=\tfrac12,1,2\), respectively; the sixth adds no exclusion. Thus all six steps are defined exactly on
\[
D=\mathbb R\setminus\left\{-1,0,\tfrac12,1,2\right\}.
\]

For every \(x\in D\), six applications return to \(x\). The same six allowed values then repeat, so no later step introduces a new restriction and \(f_{n+6}(x)=f_n(x)\). This also verifies the stated equality \(f_{35}(x)=f_5(x)\).

Since \(28=4\cdot6+4\),
\[
f_{28}(x)=f_4(x)=\boxed{\frac{1}{1-x}},\qquad x\in D.
\]
The answer is choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
solutions.title: Compute and verify a short cycle
